name: Cinnamomum zeylanicum bark extract
lead: Cinnamomum zeylanicum is an older botanical name for Cinnamomum verum, the evergreen tree of Sri Lanka known as true or Ceylon cinnamon. Its dried inner bark is the cinnamon spice, and extracts of the bark are used in supplements and in cosmetic formulations [1]. In the hair and skin-care category the extract is described as a component of the Sepicontrol A5 ingredient blend, so it reaches people mainly as one ingredient in a scalp or skin product rather than as a stand-alone treatment.

Published research on the extract concerns topics such as memory in rodents, protection against drug-induced heart injury in rats, and in-vitro antioxidant and antimicrobial activity [2][3][6][7]. No study found tests it for hair or scalp appearance.

paras: C. verum is a tree of 10-15 m in the wild; cultivated trees are kept as bushes of about 3 m, first harvested at around three years and remaining productive for decades. Sri Lanka produces roughly 80-90 percent of the world supply, and the tree is also grown in the Seychelles, Madagascar, Tanzania and parts of Borneo [1].

Workers peel the inner bark by hand into strips that dry into quills; whole long quills are valued above broken pieces, while twigs, leaves and berries are distilled for a lower-value oil. The name zeylanicum derives from Ceylon, the former name of Sri Lanka, and the name cinnamon has also been applied to Cinnamomum cassia [1].

Cinnamon has a long history in traditional medicine, including as a digestive aid [1]. A 2015 rodent paper notes traditional use of the bark for nervous stress, as a nervine tonic and as a stimulant [2].

A 2015 rodent study of a standardized aqueous bark extract, standardized by cinnamaldehyde content, examined learning and memory at 50, 100 and 200 mg/kg against streptozotocin-induced memory impairment [2]. A 2021 study in Wistar rats examined whether bark extract protected against doxorubicin-induced heart toxicity, using dexrazoxane as the positive control [6]. A 2018 study found cinnamon bark oil reduced viability of Candida albicans and caused cell-surface changes [7]. A 2023 in-vitro study characterized nanosuspensions of the extract and evaluated antioxidant, antibacterial, cytotoxic and antidiabetic activity [3]. These are not hair studies.

No studies found for hair or scalp use. Registered human trials of cinnamon bark or extract address other conditions, including type 2 diabetes (a terminated trial of cinnamon bark, water-soluble extract and metformin, n=25) [4], polycystic ovary syndrome (terminated, n=8) [5], induction of labor (n=70) [8], and weight loss with Withania (n=40) [9].

card.summary: Ceylon cinnamon bark extract, listed in a cosmetic blend, with no hair or scalp studies behind it.
card.aka: Ceylon cinnamon bark extract; Cinnamomum verum
card.note: Evidence is limited to non-cosmetic lab and rodent work.

quick.overview:
This is an extract of the inner bark of the Ceylon cinnamon tree, described as one component of the Sepicontrol A5 cosmetic blend.
Published work on it covers memory in rodents and lab antioxidant tests; none addresses hair or scalp appearance.
quick.mechanism: No mechanism for hair or scalp effects has been established.

chain: Cinnamon bark extract included in a cosmetic blend
Applied to scalp or skin in a finished product
Intended cosmetic effect attributed to the blend as a whole
angle.text: The extract is used as an ingredient in a cosmetic blend aimed at hair and scalp care. Its antioxidant and antimicrobial activity in lab tests is the kind of property sellers cite for such uses, although those tests were not done on hair or scalp.
